# Dry run: Oxford Companion attributions (62 rows) — UN-APPLIED

**Status: dry run only. No catalogue row has been changed.** Generated by
`tools/generate_companion_manifest.py` from
[`evidence/eponyms/companion-verdicts.tsv`](evidence/eponyms/companion-verdicts.tsv),
applied in dry-run by `tools/apply_attribution_manifest.py --strict --validate`.
Awaiting an explicit GO.

## The role is read from the book, not from the label

The retrieval returns a role alongside each passage, and the first draft
checked that label against the quote. That was the wrong way round. The
passage is the evidence and the label is a summary of it, so the passage
decides — and on 13 entries the two disagree. The Durkin Opening came
back "originated" against a quote reading "played in over-the-board and
correspondence games by Robert Durkin", which is a populariser.

Reading the verb requires finding the *right* verb, and two attempts
were wrong before this one.

Counting verbs across the whole quote loses the best row in the set. The
Damiano entry reads "a variation given by LUCENA and rightly condemned
by DAMIANO": two verbs, two people, and a rule that holds anything
ambiguous throws away the fact that Damiano condemned the defence which
bears his name. The verb has to be the one governing *our* person.

Locating that person by their first appearance finds the headword, since
every entry about someone opens with their name — which for the Damiano
Defence points at "given by LUCENA", Lucena's role and not Damiano's. So
the search runs over the entry body, and the window is cut back to the
clause boundary rather than a fixed width.

One pattern needed narrowing too: "re-introduced" is not origination.
The Companion says Cavallotti introduced the Albin Counter-gambit and
Albin re-introduced it, which makes Albin the populariser of his own
eponym rather than its originator.

## Asking again about one line inside a many-line entry

33 rows were held because their entry describes several openings and a
role read off the whole thing says nothing reliable about which one is
ours. Held is the right default and a poor destination, so
`tools/resolve_multi_entries.py` asks again — naming the entry and the
exact line, and requiring only the clause describing *that* line. 31 came
back resolved, and they arrive with disputes the whole-entry reading
could never have surfaced: the Caro-Kann Flohr is "an idea of
Opocensky's played twice by Flohr at Moscow 1935".

Narrowing the text does not loosen a guardrail — the clause still has to
name the person and still has to carry one unambiguous verb — and two of
the recovered rows were caught by exactly that.

The Sicilian Alapin clause reads "(sometimes called the
Alapin-Sveshnikov Variation) ... CARRERA'S interesting invention".
Alapin appears in it, but as part of an opening's name rather than as
someone doing something, and anchoring on that occurrence credited him
with Carrera's invention. The Cozio clause fails the same way: "a
variation first given by CARRERA" is Carrera's role, and reading it as
Cozio's would be a citation that contradicts itself.

So a name inside an opening's name is not the person acting, and a
person who cannot be located as an actor gets no role from that passage
at all. Both rows are held.

## How 208 candidates became 62

Five guardrails, and the two added last are the ones that matter, because
each was written after finding a row it had to reject.

| excluded | why |
|---:|---|
| 87 | the Companion has no entry for that line |
| 33 | the passage supports no single role for our person |
| 20 | the person is never named as an actor, only in a title or an opening's name |
| 6 | no answer returned |

The two in bold were added after reading the first draft's output.

`A.Kan` proposed "Paul Keres (populariser)" while its own quote says the
line has been known since the 1840s, was played by Huckle in 1851, and
never mentions Keres doing anything — his name is in the entry's title,
which is true of every entry about a person and therefore proves
nothing. Stripping the headword before checking is what catches it.

`A.Hol.Sta` proposed "Howard Staunton (originator)" against a quote
reading "played by Staunton against Horwitz in 1847" — which supports
populariser and not originator. Requiring the quote to carry a verb
consistent with the role is what catches that.

Rows carrying no verb that settles a single role for our person are held
rather than guessed at.

## What the 40 carry

38 populariser, 13 originator, 6 advocate, 4 first to publish, 1 critic.
30 record a rival claimant in `historical_notes`.

The role is the point. Every open chess dataset can say "Sicilian
Defence"; almost none can say that Damiano *condemned* the defence that
bears his name, or that Robatsch merely popularised a line known since
the sixteenth century.
